FAST

Chinese fast-fashion giant Shein will pay US$100 million to settle with the US Federal Trade Commission over claims it misled consumers on shipping times, product reviews and the origin of cotton in some of its goods, according to court documents filed on Tuesday (Nov 24). Despite marketing fast shipping, Shein knew customers were receiving packages days or months late, and in some instances not at all, the FTC said in its complaint. The company makes up around half of fast-fashion sales in the US, t he agency said. A Shein spokesperson said the company had not admitted liability and that it disagreed with some of the FTC's claims. Shein agreed to continue strengthening its consumer practices and compliance efforts as part of the settlement, the company said. Shein also agreed not to misrepresent shipping times or block negative reviews, among other changes. The FTC , which protects consumers from unfair business practices, will use the funds to reimburse c ustomers, according to court documents . REVIEW PRACTICES AND SUSTAINABILITY CLAIMS CHALLENGED

The company also filtered out negative product reviews, the FTC said. Shein internal guidance told employees to exclude "extremely bad comments", such as that a piece of jewellery would stain the customer's skin, the FTC said. The FTC also accused Shein of making misrepresentations and unsubstantiated claims about its supply chain. The company claimed products with the "evolu SHEIN " label had come from suppliers with above-average scores on social responsibility audits, but could not produce any independent audits to back the claims, the FTC said. The FTC also questioned Shein 's claims about the origin of cotton used in its US products, saying that the company's testing was often inaccurate or inconclusive. Shein has long grappled with claims that its clothes contain cotton from the Xinjiang region, where the US and human rights groups say government-sponsored forced labour programs target Uyghur minorities. Shein has previously said it does not use Chinese cotton in products sold in the US, where the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act bans any imports from Xinjiang. Shein , founded in China and headquartered in Singapore, went public in September in Hong Kong. The retailer was known for selling US$5 dresses and US$10 jeans, but it has been forced to raise its prices as the US and then Europe closed customs duty loopholes.

China's Huawei convicted in sprawling US criminal trial over Iran business

A Brooklyn federal jury convicted Huawei on 10 of 12 criminal counts over deceiving banks about Iran business and stealing US companies’ trade secrets.

A view shows a Huawei logo at Huawei Technologies France headquarters in Boulogne-Billancourt near Paris, France, Jan 9, 2025. (Photo: REUTERS/Gonzalo)

FAST

NEW YORK: Chinese telecommunications equipment maker Huawei was convicted by a jury in New York City on Tuesday (Nov 25) in a sprawling US criminal case on charges that it deceived banks about its business in Iran and stole trade secrets from American companies. The verdict came in a criminal case that began in 2018, with the US government the following year placing Huawei on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to US technology amid American concerns that Huawei posed national security risks. The jury in Brooklyn federal court found Huawei guilty on 10 of the 12 criminal counts the company faced, including bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations and conspiring to steal trade secrets. The jury acquitted Huawei of conspiring to obstruct justice and racketeering conspiracy, a charge alleging the company had acted as a criminal enterprise. The trial lasted more than two months, with prosecutors calling more than 60 witnesses and the defense calling 15. It was not immediately clear what penalties Huawei will face when US District Judge Ann Donnelly sentences it on Sep 14, 2027.

Reuters stories in 2012 and 2013 helped expose Huawei's activities in Iran and were discussed during the trial. "After the media started questioning Huawei's operations in Iran, so did Huawei's banks," prosecutor Meredith Arfa told jurors during closing arguments in the case last week. Brian Heberlig, a lawyer for Huawei, said the company was disappointed by the convictions but said the acquittal on the racketeering conspiracy charge vindicated its "good-faith compliance culture." "We fully expect to appeal," Heberlig told reporters. US Attorney Joseph Nocella said in a statement: “Few crimes are as serious as Huawei’s decades-long pattern of endangering US national security, violating the sanctity of US commerce, and impeding the enforcement of US laws.” China's embassy in Washington did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Related:

US plans to ban Chinese telecom firms from direct access to US phone numbers

Asked how much the company may have to pay in penalties, Heberlig said it was premature to comment, but said the acquittal on the racketeering conspiracy charge could make a significant difference. Experts have said the case did not undermine Huawei's business, as the company diversified and emerged as a key player in China's push for artificial intelligence. FOUNDER'S DAUGHTER WAS DETAINED In December 2018, Meng Wanzhou, Huawei's chief financial officer and daughter of the company's founder, was detained in Canada on a US warrant, prompting a diplomatic crisis involving the United States, China and Canada. Meng had been secretly indicted on US charges of misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei's business in Iran, so the company could move dollars in and out of Iran in violation of American sanctions. Meng fought extradition to the US for nearly three years, before entering a deferred prosecution agreement and flying home to China to a hero's welcome. The charges against her were dropped. Meng did not testify at trial, though an HSBC banker she met with in 2013 did testify.

Defence lawyer Brian Heberlig makes closing arguments at the Huawei Technologies trial before US District Judge Ann M. Donnelly at Brooklyn Federal Court in New York City, US, Nov 17, 2026 in this courtroom sketch. (Photo: REUTERS/Jane Rosenberg)

The 2018 indictment alleged that Huawei misled HSBC, Standard Chartered and BNP Paribas about its business dealings in Iran. Prosecutors added new charges in 2020, including allegations that Huawei conspired to steal trade secrets from US technology companies over two decades. THE PROSECUTION CASE During the trial, prosecutors sought to prove that Huawei stole source code from Cisco Systems for its routers, stole wireless telecommunications company Quintel's antenna technology, and hired a professor to gain access to a circuit board developed by semiconductor company CNEX. Jurors watched a video that, according to prosecutors, showed a Huawei employee slipping a piece of a T-Mobile testing robot into his backpack, and heard about a Huawei engineer sneaking into a Fujitsu booth at a trade show to photograph a device. Prosecutors gave jurors a statement attached to Meng's deferred prosecution agreement in which she acknowledged that the company illegally conducted business in Iran. The defense argued that HSBC and the other banks knew about Huawei's business in Iran and were competing for Huawei's business. Heberlig accused prosecutors during his closing argument of having "cherry-picked" a handful of disparate incidents to support their claim of a 20-year conspiracy. Heberlig said Huawei succeeded through "hard work, innovation, and investment in research and development". The company has more than 200,000 employees and operates in approximately 170 countries.

Source: Reuters/fs/lk

Nvidia's Jensen Huang said he violated code of conduct, source says

Addressing staff at a meeting at Nvidia's headquarters in California, CEO Jensen Huang said it was untrue that he was reinstated because of pressure from US President Donald Trump on the board.

FAST

Nvidia's reinstated CEO Jensen Huang told employees on Tuesday (Nov 24) that he had violated some of the company's code of conduct and made "some terrible mistakes", one person familiar with the matter told Reuters. Addressing staff at an hour-long all-hands meeting at Nvidia's headquarters in Santa Clara, California - a day after he returned as head of the company he co-founded three decades ago - Huang said it was untrue that he had been reinstated because of pressure from US President Donald Trump on the board, the person said. Huang said he was in therapy and acknowledged it was not acceptable to have violated aspects of Nvidia's code of conduct, the person said. Nvidia's shares closed 5.9 per cent lower as the historic rally sparked on Monday by Huang's reinstatement lost steam, with investors refocusing on the political and governance risks surrounding his return.

His resignation last week over revelations of extramarital affairs , one with an alleged Chinese spy, roiled markets and unsettled the AI ecosystem reliant on the chipmaker's technology and funding. Trump took credit forbringing back Huang. Huang apologised while disagreeing with reports that he had been an abusive boss, the New York Times reported, citing a livestream of the meeting it had reviewed. Huang also rejected claims that he returned because he was a "tech bro" and "above the law", and said he returned because Nvidia's board had evaluated facts and was assured that there was no threat to national security, NYT and Bloomberg News reported. Nvidia said in a statement on Monday that based on US government input, the board was confident that "Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk", a claim backed by Trump in an interview with CNBC.

Related:

Commentary: Jensen Huang should never have been too big to fail at Nvidia

Jensen Huang’s stunning return as Nvidia CEO: A timeline of events

US lawmakers from both parties sharply criticised Nvidia's decision, saying Congress should scrutinise the circumstances surrounding Huang's return. "The reinstatement itself raises as many questions as it answers. His return removes a major uncertainty, but what it leaves behind is an overhang on how Nvidia's governance is viewed," said Dan Sheehan, director of portfolio management at Telos Wealth Advisors. "There are also questions ... about how involved the government will be in Nvidia, and about governance of conduct internally given the stance the reinstatement implicitly took. Those don't get resolved by a soaring stock price." In an interview with the New York Post, Trump said that he's willing to pardon Huang if necessary but that he believes the reinstalled Nvidia CEO should be fine without one. Trump also told the New York Post that Nvidia's success was essential to the US retaining an edge in AI and that he's even open to the company giving the American government an equity stake, noting Intel handed more than 10 per cent of its stake last year. "I thought about it. I said, 'You know, maybe I should do it,' but I didn't bring it up at this point. It's probably not too late," Trump told the New York Post.

Related:

Jensen Huang is back, but questions facing Nvidia remain, say analysts

Nvidia board's Huang reversal raises doubts about independence, critics say

Nvidia and the White House could not immediately be reached for comment outside regular business hours. UNDER THE SCANNER Both Huang and Nvidia are facing a host of state and federal probes and reviews, including from the FBI, the Justice Department and the US Securities and Exchange Commission. A public Senate hearing is set for Dec 3, where Huang is due to testify, while the board's own investigations into potential foreign intelligence efforts, national security and export controls are still underway. "Now that the dust is beginning to settle, people are taking a more critical look at (Nvidia's) decision ... They (board) put themselves at a tremendous ethical and legal risk by the decision they made," said Peter Andersen, founder of Andersen Capital Management. Huang's upcoming testimony is also an "enormous risk to the company", he said. The surge on Monday propelled Nvidia back into second place among the world's most valuable companies, behind Apple, although the stock remains almost 31 per cent below its Oct 6 record high. AI-related companies, including chipmakers and data-center stocks, rose sharply as well, while the benchmark S&P 500 added more than US$2.8 trillion in market value. "As incredible as Monday was, I don't take it as a sign we're out of the woods ... a market that can rise US$3 trillion on one headline can fall just as fast on another," Telos' Sheehan said.

Source: Reuters/lk

item.title: Jensen Huang’s stunning return as Nvidia CEO: A timeline of events
item.description: From scandal and resignation to a comeback that sent Nvidia shares soaring 31.5 per cent in a day, CNA traces Jensen Huang’s dramatic fall and rise - and the stock’s wild ride with him.

Jensen Huang’s stunning return as Nvidia CEO: A timeline of events

From scandal and resignation to a comeback that sent Nvidia shares soaring 31.5 per cent in a day, CNA traces Jensen Huang’s dramatic fall and rise - and the stock’s wild ride with him.

Jensen Huang gestures as employees applaud his return to office after Nvidia reinstated him as the company's CEO, in Santa Clara, California, US on Nov 23, 2026. (Photo: Nvidia via X/via Reuters)

FAST

Nearly two weeks after Jensen Huang stepped down as chief executive of Nvidia , the Taiwanese-American tech billionaire on Monday (Nov 23) was reinstated as CEO in a stunning comeback . Huang had stepped down earlier this month following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy . His resignation plunged the chipmaker into crisis and sent shockwaves across an AI industry he helped bankroll. US stocks surged on Monday , with the Nasdaq jumping more than 6 per cent as Huang’s reinstatement drew investors back to AI-related shares after last week’s rout. Nvidia soared as much as 36.6 per cent after its board announced his return. Huang’s comeback followed strong public pressure for his reinstatement, including from US President Donald Trump, industry figures such as Tesla CEO Elon Musk and prominent venture capitalists. A petition calling for his reinstatement drew over 180,000 signatures.

In a statement, Huang said that he was honoured to return and "can’t wait to get back to work".  Videos circulating on social media showed the CEO - wearing a navy jacket instead of his signature black leather jacket - with his hand over his heart, looking up at employees gathered across multiple floors in the building.  "I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around," he said, amid cheers and applause.

Related:

Wall Street jumps back as Jensen Huang returns as Nvidia CEO

Inside the ‘war room’ that lobbied Donald Trump to bring back Nvidia’s Jensen Huang

Here’s a timeline of how the controversy unfolded and how Nvidia's share price has taken a wild ride with him. Oct 29: US investigation reported, Huang defends business dealings The New York Times (NYT) reported on Oct 29, 2026, that US authorities had investigated Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang , "who had a close relationship with Jensen Huang" - over suspicions that she had been "passing intelligence to Beijing" and helped circumvent US restrictions on advanced AI chips. The NYT report stated that US President Trump was "briefed and took no action". It also raised questions about Alice Huang’s relationship with the Nvidia CEO. Closing share price: US$213.66, 0.8 per cent down from Oct 28. Oct 30: Alice Huang suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence The next day, the Wall Street Journal published a report alleging that Alice Huang was suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence. "Investigators believed the woman, Alice Huang, was recruited based on her relationship with Jensen Huang," the WSJ report said, also attributing concerns to Singapore officials about her relationship with Huang and alleged intelligence connections. Speaking to Bloomberg News on Oct 30, Huang described Nvidia’s dealings with Singapore-based cloud computing firm Megaspeed as "normal and not unusual" and said that the company had checked that Megaspeed did not illegally divert Nvidia AI chips to China. "We've studied all their deployments of our GPUs and counted every one," Huang told Bloomberg - also describing his interactions with Alice Huang, who was "no longer with Megaspeed", as typical of those with Chinese customers and executives. That same day, Beijing rejected the espionage allegations, describing them as "groundless speculation" and an attempt to "smear China". Closing share price: US$204.64, 4.2 per cent down from Oct 29. Oct 31: Trump voices support for Huang On Oct 31, a Saturday, Trump voiced his support for Huang in the wake of the NYT report, calling him " brilliant ", adding that Washington was looking "very closely" at the issue. "I have a lot of respect for Jensen. I didn’t know about the specific thing, but I hope he’s going to be OK. He's a great, brilliant person, and we want to protect our brilliant people," Trump told reporters at his Florida residence. "We’re going to check it out very closely," he added. Huang has advised Trump on AI policy and was among the bevy of tech CEOs who joined the US leader on his visit to Beijing in May to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Related:

From affair allegations to Nvidia probe: How the Jensen Huang controversy unfolded

Nvidia probe: Woman in spy scandal entered Taiwan on Hong Kong passport, say authorities

Nov 4 to Nov 5: US lawmakers seek briefing from Nvidia CEO Three senior Republican lawmakers requested a closed-door briefing from Huang over the reported intelligence allegations. In a letter dated Nov 4, House Foreign Affairs Committee chairman Brian Mast, House Select Committee on China chairman John Moolenaar and House Intelligence Committee chairman Eric Crawford asked Huang to appear before them on Nov 18. According to Reuters, the lawmakers sought information about the allegations and Nvidia's procedures for protecting sensitive information from foreign intelligence operations. Nvidia responded that its chief executive regularly meets customers and business leaders worldwide, and that its cloud customers in Asia receive ordinary business information rather than sensitive trade secrets or information affecting US national security. Closing share price on Nov 5: US$181.60, 9.3 per cent down from Nov 4. Nov 8: Huang admits his infidelity In a bombshell message to Nvidia employees dropped on a Sunday, Huang admitted that he had been "unfaithful" to his wife , following reports about his alleged relationship with Alice Huang. Huang wrote that his actions had "hurt her" and their children. "There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry." He added that he took "full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused" and "accepts the criticism that comes with it". He also said that he remained "fully committed to Nvidia" and "supports the independent investigation". "I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security," Huang said. Following Huang's admission, Nvidia announced that its board was launching an independent investigation into whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. Closing share price: US$186.64 on Friday (Nov 6), 2.8 per cent up from Nov 5.

Nov 9: Trump defends Huang Following the revelations, Nvidia's stock drop wiped about US$190 billion off its market value. Meanwhile, Trump described Huang as an "honorable guy" who had "done an amazing job for our country". However, speaking to reporters, he said he had not discussed the affair allegations with Huang. "I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what is going on," he added. Chinese government officials again dismissed allegations of Chinese espionage during a routine press briefing on the same day.  "The so-called allegations of Chinese espionage are entirely baseless and amount to nothing more than smears and attempts to discredit China," said Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesperson Guo Jiakun. Closing share price: US$178.67, down 4.3 per cent from Nov 6. Nov 10: Shareholder sues Nvidia and Huang The Associated Press (AP) on Nov 10 reported that a shareholder had sued Nvidia and Huang , accusing them of deceiving investors in their responses about Huang’s affair. The complaint accused Nvidia and Huang of failing to disclose the affair and issuing false statements about Nvidia’s relationship with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which posed a “material risk” to Nvidia’s reputation and business prospects. It is common for shareholders to sue companies after unexpected share price declines. Closing share price: US$168.89, down 5.5 per cent from Nov 9.

Related:

Alice Huang in touch with Chinese spy agency during affair with Nvidia CEO: Report

US lawmakers criticise Nvidia decision to reinstate Huang as CEO

Nov 11: Alleged second affair involving Huang In another blow to Huang’s reputation, the New York Times on Nov 11 reported the tech billionaire had an extramarital affair with Kimberly Powell , the company’s vice president of health care. The report cited five people who worked at the company, and followed another report that Nvidia’s company board was preparing to oust Huang from his position. While this affair remained unconfirmed, Nvidia shares fell nearly 4 per cent in extended trading. Closing share price: US$173.73, up 2.9 per cent from Nov 10. Nov 12: Huang resigns as Nvidia CEO Huang announced his resignation as CEO of Nvidia on Nov 12, with the company’s chief financial officer Colette Kress taking over as interim CEO. Kress and longtime Nvidia engineer Ian Buck had emerged as the leading internal candidates among investors and analysts even before Huang's departure. Closing share price: US$166.19, 4.3 per cent down from Nov 11. Nov 13: US lawmakers summon Huang US lawmakers on Nov 13 summoned Huang to face their questions in December following his resignation. At this point, the scandal had wiped almost half a trillion dollars off Nvidia's market valuation, AFP reported. "Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology," Republican Senator Tim Scott wrote on X. Scott added that he was requesting Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify in December before the Senate Banking Committee, which he chairs, last week. Huang is also scheduled for a closed-door interview with three House of Representatives committees on Dec 1, on threat of subpoena. Closing share price: US$162.85, 2 per cent down from Nov 12.

Nov 16: Huang discusses comeback with allies Citing people familiar with the matter, the Financial Times on Nov 16 reported that Huang was considering a comeback as Nvidia’s CEO. One source told FT that they were putting together a "war room" of Silicon Valley executives to lobby for Huang’s return and also try to garner support from the White House. The campaign to reinstate him as CEO saw support from tech industry leaders and many of Nvidia’s employees. SpaceX and Tesla boss Elon Musk and Tim Sweeney, CEO of video game maker Epic Games, were among thousands of people who signed an online petition calling for Huang to return to the company. Trump told reporters that he would welcome Huang’s return at Nvidia. "I would certainly not mind seeing that. "I think he learned a big lesson." Closing share price: US$156.14, 4.1 per cent down from Nov 13. Nov 17: Nvidia chair says board will not rehire Huang Nvidia chairman Harvey Jones on Nov 17 said the board did not intend to reinstate Huang as CEO , despite the latter saying that he was ready to return. Hours before Nvidia’s quarterly results were released on Nov 17, Huang said he "would be honoured" to come back as CEO if the board decided his return would be in the best interest of shareholders and employees.

Jensen Huang reacts as employees applaud his return to office after Nvidia reinstated him as the company's CEO, in Santa Clara, California, US on Nov 23, 2026, in this screengrab obtained from a social media video. (Photo: Zhengzhong Tu/via Reuters)

However, Jones quashed that possibility on a call with analysts after Nvidia's earnings were released, saying the board would take the search for a new CEO "very seriously" and would consider internal and external candidates. Nvidia doubled its revenue in its third quarter to more than US$115 billion, the company reported on Nov 17, exceeding analysts' expectations.  Closing share price: US$155.46, 0.4 per cent down from Nov 16. Nov 20: Nvidia shares fall further, Trump calls for second chance Anthropic’s much-hyped arrival on Wall Street could not arrest Nvidia's slide. The record US$81 billion listing failed to dispel growing worries about the sector’s massive investments and sky-high evaluations. Traders were also spooked by the US Commerce Department's move to close a loophole allowing Chinese companies to access Nvidia's powerful AI chips remotely, adding to worries that a new Democratic-led Congress will impose further restrictions on the sector. Meanwhile, Trump again sang Huang's praises, saying that the former CEO should be "given a second chance". "I would love to see him be back. You have one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world, and where is he going to go?" Trump told reporters. "I think that I would love to see Jensen be given a second chance."
